analysis.one_liner: Requires the largest freight railroads to give their workers seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill to guarantee freight rail workers seven paid sick days a year sat in committee for the entire Congress and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the biggest freight railroads to give every employee at least seven days of paid sick leave per year, distinct from vacation or personal days, with unused days carrying over. Workers could use it for their own illness or doctor visits, to care for family, or to deal with domestic violence or stalking. Railroads could not discipline workers for taking the leave or make them find their own replacements first. As an enforcement backstop, the Department of Transportation could not approve a railroad's safety risk reduction plan unless the carrier complied with the sick leave requirement.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 100,000 workers at the Class I freight railroads (Union Pacific, BNSF, CSX, Norfolk Southern and peers) would gain a guaranteed seven paid sick days a year — leave they could use for themselves or a family member without losing pay, being disciplined under attendance policies, or having to find their own replacement. Rail riders and communities near rail lines would also benefit indirectly: the bill ties federal safety plan approval to compliance, on the theory that rested, healthy crews make fewer catastrophic errors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Freight rail workers and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires each Class I freight railroad to give employees at least seven paid sick days a year, with unused days carrying over — vacation and personal days cannot be repackaged as sick leave.
Lets workers use the leave for their own illness, doctor and preventive care, care for family, or absences from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
Bars railroads from disciplining, demoting, or counting attendance points against a worker who takes the leave, and from requiring the worker to find their own replacement before taking it.
Adds teeth: the Transportation Department cannot approve a railroad's federally required safety risk reduction plan unless the carrier complies with the sick leave rules.

analysis.who_pays: The Class I freight railroads, which would bear the cost of a new paid leave mandate and lose a management tool: attendance point systems and the practice of requiring a worker to find their own replacement would be off-limits for sick leave. Those costs could eventually show up in shipping rates or service levels.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises labor costs for the largest freight railroads, which could face pressure to slow hiring or raise rates to cover new paid-leave obligations; that cost objection is the industry's principal argument against mandated sick leave.
It covers only Class I railroad employees rather than establishing paid sick leave for other workers, leaving most of the workforce without the same guarantee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to roughly a hundred thousand railroad workers and their families are concrete and modest: guaranteed paid sick days usable for themselves or family, with anti-retaliation teeth. The main honest objection is cost and flexibility for the railroads, and the bill's narrowness — it addresses one workforce rather than the broader lack of paid sick leave. But the railroads' record attendance policies that discipline sick workers are precisely what the bill targets, and the safety argument (rested, uninfected crews) gives the public a direct stake.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's railroads subcommittee in May 2023 and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Donald Payne Jr. introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, and it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials — the last action of any kind recorded for the bill.
It gathered 53 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill ever leaving committee or receiving a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Class I freight railroads are better off: they avoid a federal mandate for paid sick days and keep full control over attendance and discipline policies. Rail workers who were counting on the legislation got nothing.

for.name: 53 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: All 53 cosponsors of the bill were Democrats; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Class I freight railroads (BNSF, Union Pacific, CSX, Norfolk Southern)
against.what_they_did: The major railroads opposed federally mandated sick leave during the 2022 national contract dispute, when only one of twelve unions' proposed sick day provisions survived the bargaining process.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: The committee, controlled by the House's majority party, referred the bill to its railroads subcommittee and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 53 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with the House under Republican control in the 118th Congress, the bill never advanced out of committee.

industries.note: The bill requires the largest freight railroads to provide at least seven paid sick days a year and restricts their attendance and discipline practices; it also conditions federal safety plan approval on compliance. In 2022, the same carriers had resisted adding paid sick leave in national contract negotiations.
Rail unions had made paid sick leave a central demand; the bill sets a federal floor while leaving additional days to collective bargaining under the Railway Labor Act.
